clinical_procedures.name: Thoracentesis (diagnostic and therapeutic)
steps: Position patient sitting upright; consider lateral decubitus if unstable.
Perform consent and time-out; mark correct side.
Use ultrasound in real time to localize effusion and optimal intercostal space.
Prep skin with chlorhexidine or betadine; place sterile drape; wear mask and sterile gloves.
Anesthetize skin and intercostal tract with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine using 25-gauge then 22-gauge 2.5-in needle.
Make a small subcutaneous stab incision with #11 scalpel.
Insert needle-with-catheter above the rib into pleural space with continuous aspiration; advance catheter over needle, then withdraw needle.
Drain fluid with one-way syringe and tubing; consider Vacutainer/wall suction cautiously due to possible increased complications.
Monitor symptoms and, if using manometry, stop if Ppl < −20 cmH2O, or if patient develops chest discomfort/cough/shoulder pain, or when no more fluid.
Remove catheter during exhalation; cover site with sterile dressing; consider post-procedure ultrasound; chest radiograph only if suspicion for pneumothorax.
notes: Place needle on the superior margin of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
Ultrasound guidance reduces pneumothorax risk and increases success after a dry tap.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Pleural fluid analysis
details: Classify as transudate vs exudate using Light’s criteria.
Additional tests as indicated: glucose, pH, amylase, cholesterol, albumin, rheumatoid factor, BNP, ADA.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Imaging
details: Chest radiograph patterns (bilateral vs unilateral; nodules; interstitial infiltrates) suggest etiologies.
Thoracic ultrasound: guidance for thoracentesis; predictive of trapped lung/entrapment via lung motion and pleural thickening.

recommendations: Evaluate any new, unexplained pleural effusion with thoracentesis unless typical CHF is obvious.
Combine diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis in a single setting when feasible.
Correct bleeding disorders when possible; small-bore needle may be used with anticoagulation or uremia when benefits outweigh risks.
Avoid areas of skin infection; mechanical ventilation is not a contraindication.
Use real-time ultrasound guidance to reduce complications.
Routine chest radiograph is not required; obtain if air aspiration, multiple unsuccessful attempts, or prior thoracic radiation or other high-risk scenarios.
Stop drainage if Ppl drops below −20 cmH2O, if no more fluid, or if patient develops chest discomfort.
Large volumes can be drained safely when monitoring symptoms and/or Ppl.

drug_information.name: Lidocaine 1%
notes: Without epinephrine. Avoid injecting once pleural fluid aspirated.

definitions.definition: Drainage of fluid from the pleural cavity.
Accumulation of fluid in the pleural space causing cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain.
Intrapleural pressure measured during thoracentesis (pleural liquid pressure).
Re-expansion pulmonary edema; risk increases when Ppl drops below −20 cmH2O.
Non-expandable lung due to visceral pleural scarring; often transudative and asymptomatic.
Non-expandable lung due to visceral pleural thickening or obstruction; typically exudative and symptomatic.
Biochemical criteria distinguishing exudate from transudate: pleural LDH > 2/3 ULN serum, pleural/serum LDH >0.6, pleural/serum protein >0.5; one criterion suffices.
Functional residual capacity; steady-state Ppl approximately −3 to −5 cmH2O.
B-type natriuretic peptide; may be measured in pleural fluid.
Adenosine deaminase; may be measured in pleural fluid.

clinical_pearls: Always insert needle on the superior rib margin to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
Use real-time ultrasound guidance to reduce pneumothorax risk and increase success.
Stop drainage for chest pain, intense cough, dyspnea, or when Ppl < −20 cmH2O.
Routine post-thoracentesis chest radiograph is unnecessary without specific risk factors.
Remove the catheter during exhalation to minimize air entry.

clinical_applications: Thoracentesis provides diagnostic clarity and symptom relief in pleural effusions.
Real-time ultrasound improves safety and success.
practice_recommendations: Combine diagnostic and therapeutic thoracentesis when possible.
Use ultrasound guidance; avoid routine chest radiograph post-procedure.
Monitor symptoms and Ppl during large-volume drainage; stop if Ppl < −20 cmH2O or discomfort.
future_directions: Clarify safety implications of suction-assisted drainage vs gravity/manual across settings.
Define when pleural manometry meaningfully changes outcomes.
controversies: Utility of routine manometry during thoracentesis.
Safety profile of active suction vs manual drainage in large-volume thoracentesis.

technology_and_technique.name: Pleural manometry
benefits: Guides drainage volume to avoid RPE

technology_and_technique.name: Drainage method
notes: Suction may be faster but some studies report higher complications; evidence mixed (GRAVITAS no difference in discomfort).

points: Thoracentesis is safe and effective for diagnosis and symptom relief in pleural effusions.
Ultrasound guidance and attention to pleural pressures minimize complications.
Large volumes can be drained safely when monitoring for symptoms and Ppl thresholds.
